conventions.convention: Left integrals satisfy hΛ = ε(h)Λ; right integrals satisfy Λh = ε(h)Λ. Both spaces include zero.
The dual product is convolution (f*g)(h) = Σf(h₁)g(h₂), and its counit is f ↦ f(1). A left integral functional satisfies f*λ = f(1)λ.
The regular-dual right action is (f ↼ h)(x) = f(xS(h)); the right coaction satisfies Σp(f₁)f₀(x) = Σp(x₁)f(x₂). Its coinvariants are left integral functionals.
A Frobenius pairing is β(a,b) = λ(ab); nondegeneracy requires both induced maps to the full algebraic dual to be isomorphisms.
Semisimplicity means semisimplicity of the left regular module. The criterion concerns H itself, without asserting semisimplicity of H* or involutivity of S.
The Sweedler example uses characteristic different from 2, H₄ = T₂ with ζ = −1, ordered basis (1,g,x,gx), and λ extracting the gx coefficient.

load_bearing.statement: For a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra H, the action (f ↼ h)(x) = f(xS(h)) and the uniquely specified coaction Σp(f₁)f₀(x) = Σp(x₁)f(x₂) make H* a right-right Hopf module. Its coinvariants are exactly the left integral functionals.

Let H be a nonzero finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field k. Each of the left- and right-integral spaces of H and H* is one-dimensional. The antipodes of H and H* are bijective; each sends the left-integral space isomorphically onto the right-integral space.
A nonzero finite-dimensional Hopf algebra H over a field k is semisimple as a ring if and only if there exists a left integral Λ with ε(Λ) ≠ 0. In that case Λ can be normalized so that ε(Λ) = 1.

Left integrals satisfy hΛ = ε(h)Λ for every h; right integrals satisfy Λh = ε(h)Λ. In finite dimension, left integral functionals satisfy f*λ = f(1)λ for every f ∈ H*, and right integral functionals satisfy λ*f = f(1)λ. Zero is allowed.

alerts.finding: In Proof 1.2, the counit calculation reads “$(\operatorname{id}_V\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(v\otimes h)=v\otimes h$”. Here ρ has codomain (V ⊗ H) ⊗ H, whereas id_V ⊗ ε has domain V ⊗ H. The counit contraction needs id_(V ⊗ H) ⊗ ε. The surrounding formula and conclusion make the intended contraction clear.

seams_checked.note: The integral theorem uses finite algebra-coalgebra biduality only for finite-dimensional H. The evaluation map preserves the multiplication and counit needed to transport integral equations; tensor-factor order is unchanged.

The regular-dual and averaging proofs use the stated antipode contractions, anti-multiplication, anti-comultiplication and counit preservation. Bijectivity is derived later, without assuming it in these constructions.

The dual Hopf structure is used with its exact convolution product, transposed coproduct and antipode f ↦ f ∘ S. The Taft and Sweedler examples agree with gx = ζxg and the supplier's PBW multiplication.

The regular-dual construction satisfies the supplier's right-right compatibility. The integral and Frobenius proofs apply precisely the action isomorphism M^(co H) ⊗ H → M, without adding an inverse-antipode hypothesis.

The double definition, coalgebra/antipode lemma, module-equivalence theorem and canonical-R theorem cite only finite-dimensional antipode bijectivity. Each explicitly verifies H ≠ 0 from ε(1_H) = 1_k, matching the cited theorem's hypothesis.
